name: Pinnacles National Park
tagline: Volcanic spires, talus caves and condors soaring overhead.
intro: Pinnacles is a landscape of rocky spires, narrow canyons and caves formed by tumbled boulders, where endangered California condors ride the air above the High Peaks. Its trails range from a family loop past a quiet reservoir to a climb along carved rock steps high among the spires. Scattering ashes requires a special use permit, applied for well in advance.
scatterSummary: Scattering cremation ashes requires a special use permit; the park does not publish designated locations.
scatterFacts: Special use permit required for scattering cremation ashes (Superintendent's Compendium, 36 CFR 2.62(b)).
The application should reach the park no less than 90 days before your date. Email the park to receive a copy of the application, and read the permit conditions before you arrive.
No designated scattering areas are published; ask the park where scattering may take place.
beforeYouGo: No road connects the East and West entrances; the shortest route between them is through King City on Highway 101. East Entrance (Pinnacles Visitor Center): Highway 25 south through Hollister, then Highway 146; Bear Gulch is 3.5 miles farther in. West Entrance: Highway 101 to Soledad, then 14 miles east on Highway 146, which becomes a one-lane road. Online maps may send you to the wrong side; the park publishes GPS coordinates for each entrance. In summer avoid hiking from 10 am to 4 pm; there is no water along any trail.

destinations.name: Bear Gulch Reservoir
destinations.description: This loop packs much of Pinnacles into a short morning: rock formations, talus caves, a stone staircase climbing through a narrow canyon, and then the still water of Bear Gulch Reservoir tucked among the rocks. The return along the Rim Trail opens panoramic views over the gulch. The park suggests it as a family hike, so grandchildren and grandparents can share it. Pause beside the reservoir and let the quiet water hold your memories for a while.

plan.accessibility: Dirt and rock trail 2.5 to 4 ft wide with stairs; flashlight needed if you pass through the cave (NPS)
plan.scattering: Only under a park permit; ask the park where

drive.route: Enter by the East Entrance off Highway 25 and drive about 4 miles on the park road to the Bear Gulch Day Use Area. The trail starts from the Moses Spring Parking Area near the Bear Gulch Nature Center.

trail.name: Moses Spring Trail to Rim Trail Loop
steps: Hike up Bear Gulch on the Moses Spring Trail, passing over the caves.
Climb the rock staircase to the reservoir.
Return along the Rim Trail above the gulch.
notes: Bear Gulch Cave is open seasonally and may close briefly in winter due to flooding; check its status before you go. Limited shade, none on the Rim Trail.

links.label: Moses Spring Trail to Rim Trail Loop

destinations.name: Condor Gulch Overlook
destinations.description: Sweeping views begin almost as soon as you start up Condor Gulch, and after a mile the overlook puts the High Peaks right above you. This is a favorite spot for watching birds, and with luck the park's resident condors will be riding the air over the spires. Bring binoculars and something to sit on, and give the sky time. There is something fitting about looking up together and watching those great wings circle.

plan.distance: About 2 mi round trip to the overlook
plan.accessibility: Dirt and rock trail 2 to 4 ft wide; no shade (NPS)
plan.scattering: Only under a park permit; ask the park where

drive.route: Enter by the East Entrance off Highway 25 and follow the park road 4 miles to the Bear Gulch Day Use Area. The trailhead is near the Nature Center.

trail.name: Condor Gulch Trail
steps: Climb the Condor Gulch Trail about 1 mile to the viewpoint, then return the same way.
notes: In summer the High Peaks area can be 10 degrees hotter than the parking areas; avoid the hottest part of the day and carry plenty of water.

destinations.name: Balconies Cliffs and Cave
destinations.description: Part hike, part adventure, this loop climbs up and over the Balconies Cliffs and then threads back through Balconies Cave, a passage beneath huge boulders that have toppled into a narrow canyon. Flashlights come out, voices echo, and everyone helps everyone else over the rocks. It suits a family that loves a little exploring. Afterward, stop in the sunlight below the cliffs and talk about the adventures your loved one led you on over the years.

plan.accessibility: Dirt and rock; scrambling in the cave with low ceilings, slippery rocks and uneven footing. Flashlight required (NPS)
plan.scattering: Only under a park permit; ask the park where

drive.route: Enter by the West Entrance: Highway 101 to Soledad, then Highway 146 (one-lane in places) to the Chaparral Parking Area.

trail.name: Balconies Cliffs Trail and Balconies Cave Trail
steps: From the parking area, take the connector to the Balconies Trail.
At the junction, stay right on the Balconies Cliffs Trail, up and over the cave.
Descend to the Old Pinnacles Trail and Balconies Cave Trail junction and return through the cave, then back on the Balconies Trail.
notes: Wading may be needed in winter, and the cave may close for short periods due to flooding.

destinations.name: High Peaks
destinations.description: This is the heart of Pinnacles: a climb up Condor Gulch into the rock spires, then along the Steep and Narrow section, where steps are carved into the stone and a handrail guides you along the cliffs. The park says it gives you the feeling of walking on top of the world, and condors often soar among these rocks. It is a demanding day for the strongest walkers in your family, and a high, rocky place worth carrying a memory to.

plan.accessibility: Steep dirt and rock trail 2 to 4 ft wide; carved steps with handrails on the Steep and Narrow section; no shade
plan.scattering: Only under a park permit; ask the park where

drive.route: Enter by the East Entrance off Highway 25 and stay left at the fork to the Bear Gulch Day Use Area.

trail.name: Condor Gulch Trail to High Peaks Trail Loop
steps: Climb the Condor Gulch Trail past the overlook to the High Peaks Trail.
Cross the High Peaks, including the Steep and Narrow section.
Descend back to Bear Gulch. Adding the Rim and Moses Spring trails extends the loop to 6.2 mi.
notes: The park suggests ages 7 and older. In summer the High Peaks can be 10 degrees hotter than the parking areas; keep a safe distance from condors.

links.label: Condor Gulch to High Peaks Loop
